opus-5.5.text:
Well, my strong suspicion is that the first system that really gets to human-level general intelligence won't be just a scaled-up large language model. LLMs are amazing, and they've surprised a lot of people, including me to some extent, but they're fundamentally very sophisticated pattern-recognizers over huge amounts of human-generated data. They're great at recombining what's already out there, but they're weak at the kind of creative leaps, grounded reasoning, and self-directed learning that I think are the core of general intelligence.

What I think will get us there is some kind of hybrid, integrative architecture, what I've called "cognitive synergy." You have different learning and reasoning mechanisms: neural networks for perception and pattern recognition, probabilistic logical reasoning for abstraction and inference, evolutionary learning for creative program search, and so on. They all operate on a common knowledge representation, so they can help each other out when one gets stuck. In our OpenCog Hyperon work, that common substrate is a big weighted, labeled metagraph we call the Atomspace, and we've built a language, MeTTa, so the system can represent and rewrite its own cognitive processes. That self-modification and reflection piece is crucial, I think.

So my bet is an architecture where LLMs and other deep neural nets are important components, almost like specialized cortical modules, embedded in a broader framework that does symbolic reasoning, goal-driven motivation, and open-ended self-improvement. Will the first AGI come from exactly our system? I'd love that, of course, but I'm not dogmatic about it. I'm fairly confident, though, that it'll be this kind of neural-symbolic, multi-paradigm design rather than one monolithic network trained end to end. And I care a lot about it being developed in a decentralized, open way rather than locked inside one or two big companies, but maybe we'll get to that later.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I've been thinking about this question for a few decades now, and my views have evolved, but the core of my answer has stayed fairly stable. I don't think the first human-level AGI is going to come from a single algorithm, a single learning method scaled up to enormous size. I think it's going to come from what you might call a hybrid or integrative architecture, where you have multiple different kinds of AI components, each doing what it's good at, and the magic is in how they're wired together and how they learn to cooperate.

So in the OpenCog Hyperon work that my colleagues and I have been doing, the center of the system is a large, dynamically updating knowledge metagraph. You have deep neural networks for perception and pattern recognition, you have probabilistic logic for reasoning, you have evolutionary learning for creative exploration, and all of these are operating on and feeding back into that shared representation. Each of those methods, on its own, has well-understood limitations. Neural nets are great at compressing statistical regularities in big datasets but they're not great at precise, multi-step reasoning or at learning from one example. Logic systems are great at that kind of reasoning but they're brittle and they don't learn well from raw sensory data. The hypothesis, which goes back to the cognitive synergy ideas I was writing about in the early 2000s, is that these weaknesses are complementary, so that when one method gets stuck, another one can step in and get it unstuck.

Now, the large language models of the last few years have obviously shifted the landscape. They do a lot more than I would have predicted a transformer trained to predict the next token would do. But I still see the same fundamental gaps. They don't have a robust model of the world that they're maintaining and updating. They don't have a persistent self-model or the ability to carry out long chains of inference reliably. They don't have real agency or motivation in the sense a human mind does. So I think LLMs are going to be a very important component of the first AGI systems, maybe the component that handles language and a lot of common-sense knowledge, but they're not going to be the whole thing. They'll be a module, plugged into a larger cognitive architecture with symbolic reasoning, with episodic memory, with goal systems and attention allocation.

I'd also say the architecture has to be designed so the system can rewrite and improve itself, because human-level is not where this stops. Whatever we build first is going to be a stepping-stone to something considerably beyond human level fairly quickly. So we want the first AGI to be reflective, to understand its own code and its own reasoning, and ideally to be grounded in some kind of ethical and compassionate value system before that recursive improvement really takes off. That's why I care so much about doing this in an open, decentralized way rather than inside one or two companies.

But if you're asking me to bet, I'd bet on a neural-symbolic-evolutionary hybrid with a shared knowledge representation at its core, not on any one of those methods alone. And I'd guess it emerges from a combination of a well-designed architecture and the system being embedded in a rich enough environment, interacting with people and with the world, that it has something worth being generally intelligent about.

astra-6.text:
My best guess is that it’s going to be a hybrid architecture, with several different kinds of learning and reasoning operating together. Deep neural networks are very useful for recognizing patterns, but you also want explicit reasoning, you want the ability to build and manipulate models of the world, and you want some way of grounding all that in experience and action.

The key isn’t just putting those components in the same box. It’s getting them to help each other. When one learning process gets stuck, another should be able to reformulate the problem so that it can make progress. That’s what I mean by cognitive synergy.

You’d want a shared representation of knowledge, so that something learned through perception can be used in reasoning, and something discovered through reasoning can guide perception or action. And the system needs to learn about itself as part of the world, including its own limitations and how to overcome them.

Now, I wouldn’t claim that this is the only possible route. The space of possible minds is probably enormous. But if you’re asking what seems most plausible to me as a practical engineering approach, it’s that sort of integrated, self-organizing cognitive system.

sol-6.1.text:
My best guess is that it’s going to be a hybrid architecture. I don’t think intelligence is fundamentally just reasoning, or just learning patterns, or just optimizing a reward function. You need a system where those different processes can help one another.

That’s the intuition behind our work on OpenCog. You have a common representation of knowledge, and then you have different cognitive processes acting on it: probabilistic reasoning, evolutionary learning, neural learning, and so forth. The important thing isn’t simply putting those components in the same box. It’s getting what I call cognitive synergy, where one process can get past an obstacle by drawing on the strengths of another.

I’d also expect that system to learn through interaction with a world, including other minds, rather than having all its knowledge programmed in. It needs to connect perception and action with abstract concepts, and develop some understanding of itself.

Now, is that the only possible route? Certainly not. I’m much more confident that there are multiple architectures capable of human-level general intelligence than I am that any particular one will get there first. But a hybrid system with that kind of cognitive synergy is where I would place my bet.
